content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define active transport and explain how it differs from diffusion and osmosis
Explain why active transport requires energy
Describe examples of active transport in living organisms
Compare active transport with passive transport processes

Active transport is essential for many life processes, from absorbing minerals in plant roots to transmitting nerve impulses.

content.text: Diffusion and osmosis occur naturally because of random particle movement. Moving substances against the concentration gradient is like pushing a ball uphill - it requires energy input.

attrs.alt: Step-by-step process of active transport using a carrier protein

content.text: The substance to be transported binds to a specific carrier protein on one side of the membrane
ATP is broken down, releasing energy
The energy causes the carrier protein to change shape
The substance is released on the other side of the membrane
The carrier protein returns to its original shape, ready for the next molecule
1. Mineral Ion Uptake in Plant Roots
Mineral ions (e.g., nitrate, potassium, magnesium) are more concentrated inside root hair cells than in the soil
Ions cannot enter by diffusion (wrong direction)
Root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil
Carrier proteins in the cell membrane transport specific ions
Energy comes from respiration in the root cells
This is why roots need oxygen (for respiration)

attrs.alt: Root hair cell showing active transport of mineral ions from soil

content.text: 2. Glucose Absorption in the Small Intestine
After a meal, glucose concentration in gut may be lower than in blood
Need to absorb all remaining glucose, not just until equilibrium
Epithelial cells of the villi use active transport to absorb glucose
This ensures maximum absorption of nutrients

attrs.alt: Villus showing active transport of glucose from gut lumen into blood

content.text: Good blood supply (maintains gradient, removes absorbed nutrients)
Many mitochondria in epithelial cells (ATP for active transport)
Useful substances (glucose, amino acids, some ions) are filtered into kidney tubules
These need to be reabsorbed back into the blood
Cells lining the kidney tubules use active transport
Reabsorb glucose, amino acids, and salts from the filtrate
Requires significant energy - kidneys use about 10% of body's oxygen
Nerve cells need to maintain a difference in ion concentrations across their membrane
Pumps 3 Na⁺ ions out for every 2 K⁺ ions pumped in
Maintains the resting potential of neurones

attrs.alt: Sodium-potassium pump in a neurone membrane

content.text: Sugars (sucrose) need to enter phloem sieve tubes for transport
Concentration in phloem may already be high
Companion cells use active transport to load sucrose into phloem
This drives the movement of sugars around the plant (translocation)
How do we know active transport uses energy?
When cells are treated with substances that stop respiration (e.g., cyanide), active transport stops
Active transport rate increases with temperature (up to a point), as enzyme-controlled respiration increases
Tissues doing active transport need oxygen for aerobic respiration
Cells doing lots of active transport have many mitochondria (e.g., root hair cells, gut epithelium)
Adding ATP can restore active transport in damaged cells
Cells that carry out a lot of active transport have many mitochondria because:
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration
ATP provides energy for active transport
More mitochondria = more ATP = more active transport capacity
